q: Does buying a new machine go in Scope 3 Category 1 or Category 2, and in which year?
title: New machine: Category 1 or 2?
short: A machine you capitalise as a fixed asset goes in Category 2, capital goods, with all its cradle-to-gate emissions in the year you acquire it. Parts, tools and consumables you expense go in Category 1. Follow your own accounts: the GHG Protocol tells companies to use their financial accounting treatment to draw the line.

sections.h: The rule for drawing the line
p: The Scope 3 Standard defines capital goods as final products with an extended life that a company uses to make products or provide services, and tells companies to follow their financial accounting: if it is capitalised in the fixed asset register, it is Category 2; if it is expensed, it is Category 1.

ul: New CNC machine, press, compressor, boiler, forklift: Category 2.
Replacement motor or gearbox that you capitalise: Category 2; if expensed as repairs: Category 1.
Cutting tools, dies you write off in the year, lubricants, spares: Category 1.
Building and civil works for a new shed: Category 2.
A machine taken on lease rather than bought: not Category 1 or 2; Scope 1 and 2 or Category 8, depending on your boundary approach.

p: The year of acquisition, in full. It is not spread over the asset's life as depreciation would be. If a machine is delivered in March and installed in May, use the date it is recorded as acquired in your accounts, and apply that rule every year.

A large purchase can make Category 2 jump in one year and fall the next. Report it as it is, explain the purchase in a note, and keep it out of any intensity metric you use to show operational improvement, or show that metric both with and without it.

senseible: Senseible classifies invoice lines by HSN code, so a machine invoice under chapter 84 sits in the Scope 3 trail as a likely capital good, flagged for you to confirm whether it was capitalised. It does not read your fixed asset register; that confirmation comes from your accounts team.
